justification_text:
My point estimates across all three horizons reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook with only modest drift upward over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 983 likely anchored closely to the most recent observed value, assuming mean-reverting behavior and no imminent catalysts. The slight upward drift to 987 at one week and 995 at one month reflects a gentle positive trend assumption — perhaps based on underlying momentum or a modest growth prior — while still keeping the estimates relatively close to the starting point. The flatness of the trajectory suggests I was not pricing in any strong directional signal, rather treating the series as one that fluctuates around a slowly drifting level.

The confidence interval widths widen sensibly as the horizon extends, which reflects the fundamental principle that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 56 units, which is relatively tight and reflects the low typical day-to-day variability I assumed. By one week, that span grows to about 95 units, and by one month it reaches 190 units, roughly tripling the daily range. This progression was likely informed by an assumption about the volatility or standard deviation of the underlying series, scaled by the square root of time in a manner consistent with a random walk or similar model. The intervals also reflect parameter uncertainty — I may not have had high confidence in the trend assumption itself, which adds width beyond pure noise.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive shock — such as a strong data release, policy announcement, or demand surge — could rapidly push values above 1035 or even 1090. On the downside, a sharp deterioration in conditions, an unexpected negative event, or a structural break in the underlying dynamics could drive values well below 955 or 900. These tail risks are by definition underweighted in symmetric interval construction, meaning the true distribution may have fatter tails than my confidence intervals imply.

Finally, model misspecification is itself a source of risk that sits outside the stated intervals. If the underlying process is not as stable as I assumed — for instance, if it is subject to regime changes, seasonal effects, or nonlinear dynamics — then even my widest interval at one month may be overconfident. Black swan events or sudden structural shifts are the hardest to capture in any probabilistic forecast, and they represent the primary reason real-world outcomes sometimes fall dramatically outside well-reasoned confidence bounds.
